answer.summary: Pfeffer says breaking conventional rules can make you memorable and differentiate you from people or businesses following the status quo; to succeed, choose differences that play to your strengths and help you perform. [S1, S2]

sections.heading: Why rule-breaking can build power
sections.content: Unexpected behavior makes you stand out and become memorable. Pfeffer also notes that existing rules are mostly made by people favored by the status quo, so following them may preserve incumbents’ advantages. In business, disruption comes from doing things differently from industry incumbents. [S1]

sections.heading: How to apply it
sections.content: Pfeffer’s advice is to choose differences that play to your strengths and can make you more successful—not to break rules for its own sake. His examples include Southwest not using a hub-and-spoke model, Amazon emphasizing exceptional customer service, and Whole Foods fitting local tastes rather than optimizing store costs. He also challenges the convention against asking for help: people may overestimate how many asks it will take, and asking can create opportunities they would otherwise miss. [S1, S2, S4]

sections.heading: Example: Jason Calacanis
sections.content: Pfeffer says Calacanis defied venture-capital conventions by making many small bets rather than a few large ones and running a lean operation without partners. Pfeffer presents him as someone who consistently breaks rules and became powerful in the internet industry. [S3]

judgment.explanation: The answer covers both requested reasons: unconventional behavior makes someone stand out and memorable, and existing rules tend to favor those already advantaged, so doing things differently can disrupt the status quo and support success. Its examples and practical advice are supported by the cited transcript excerpts. It does not claim that any detail is missing.
